findings.source_passage: that antique Crockett and Kit Carson—that brawny doer of rejoicing good deeds, was swallowed down and thrown up by a whale
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves the Crockett/Kit Carson phrase but drops 'I claim him for one of our clan,' which is a distinct voice moment capping the ironic admission of Hercules; its omission mutes the rhetorical wit.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'I claim him for one of our clan.' at the close of the Hercules passage.

findings.source_passage: placed before the strict and piercing truth, this whole story will fare like that fish, flesh, and fowl idol of the Philistines, Dagon by name; who being planted before the ark of Israel, his horse's head and both the palms of his hands fell off from him, and only the stump or fishy part of him remained
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reduces this to a brief allusion ('horse's head and palms off, the fishy stump remains'), losing the interpretive elaboration about Dagon as 'fish, flesh, and fowl idol' and the full ironic-exegetical machinery Melville constructs; this is a signature rhetorical set-piece.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full Dagon sentence including 'fish, flesh, and fowl idol of the Philistines, Dagon by name' and the clause specifying the precise bodily parts that 'fell off.'

findings.source_passage: when Brahma, or the God of Gods, saith the Shaster, resolved to recreate the world after one of its periodical dissolutions, he gave birth to Vishnoo, to preside over the work; but the Vedas, or mystical books, whose perusal would seem to have been indispensable to Vishnoo before beginning the creation, and which therefore must have contained something in the shape of practical hints to young architects
findings.why_it_matters: The draft collapses the full Vishnoo cosmogony—including the comic aside about 'practical hints to young architects'—to a bare clause ('when the Vedas lay at the bottom'), erasing both the voice and the interpretive scaffolding about creation and the role of Brahma.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the 'practical hints to young architects' aside and Brahma's role in the Vishnoo cosmogony; these carry Melville's signature mock-scholarly irony.

findings.source_passage: Was not this Vishnoo a whaleman, then? even as a man who rides a horse is called a horseman?
findings.why_it_matters: The draft drops the analogical coda 'even as a man who rides a horse is called a horseman,' which is a small but characteristic piece of Ishmael's mock-logical rhetoric.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the horseman analogy to the Vishnoo conclusion.

summary: Three medium-severity findings (loss of the Dagon set-piece's signature elaboration, erasure of the 'practical hints to young architects' Vishnoo aside, and omission of 'I claim him for one of our clan') together trigger regeneration under the three-medium threshold.
